paragraphs.text: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena tied to former chief executive Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The California Department of Justice announced the step on Thursday, November 19, 2026, according to the Associated Press.

According to the AP, the state is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China, and whether the company misled investors and the public. Newsweek reported that Bonta's office said the subpoena seeks information to determine whether Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, broke state law.

In a statement quoted by the AP, Bonta said the conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive "raises bright red flags." He said his office is investigating whether the actions of Nvidia or Huang resulted in China obtaining advanced chips, and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public about that risk in violation of the law.

Bonta described the company as being in a messy situation that crosses borders, but said the principle behind corporate securities law is simple. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," he said, according to the AP.

Newsweek noted that the subpoena is an investigative measure and not a finding of wrongdoing. It also reported that Bonta had told Bloomberg Television two days earlier that his office was examining the scandal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday, the AP reported.

Newsweek reported that a New York Times story on October 29 linked Huang to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of working for China's Ministry of State Security. Newsweek added that no publicly disclosed evidence has established that Huang knowingly helped Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation the week before the subpoena, after he had led the company for 33 years, and chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim chief executive, according to Newsweek. Huang later wrote on X that he would be honored to return as CEO if the board decided it was in shareholders' interest. Newsweek reported that the board, through chairman Harvey Jones, said it had unanimously accepted his resignation and did not intend to reinstate him.

The investigation lands as Nvidia's business keeps growing. Newsweek reported that the company posted record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, more than double the year before, and forecast $130 billion for the fourth quarter. Nvidia recorded $2.4 billion in third quarter sales of Hopper chips to China, and Kress said the company had stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips there. Nvidia also created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, Newsweek said.

Huang has voluntarily agreed to transcribed interviews with House lawmakers and is scheduled to appear before congressional committees on December 1, the AP reported. Newsweek said three House committees are involved. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is set to follow on December 2.

The California inquiry adds a state securities angle to a case that had largely been treated as a national security matter. Its focus on what investors were told means Nvidia's disclosures about the affair and its China business, not only Huang's personal conduct, are now under formal review.
The next public test comes on December 1, when Huang is due before House committees and may be asked the same questions about chips and China that Bonta's office is now pursuing.
